title: Memory allocation: malloc, arenas and why RSS grows
goal: By the end you can explain how malloc carves the memory it gets with brk and mmap, why freed memory usually stays in RSS, what glibc's arenas trade, and how to account for a JVM's RSS with NMT.

warmup.q: A C program mallocs 200,000 blocks of 1,000 bytes (about 192 MB), then frees every one of them except the block it allocated last. What happens to its RSS?
options: It drops to a few MB: `free` hands the memory back to the kernel
It stays at about 195 MB
It halves, because glibc returns memory in big steps
It drops at the next garbage collection
warmup.why: `free` returns chunks to malloc's free lists, not to the kernel. The heap can shrink only from the top, by moving the program break down, and the one live block at the top pins all 192 MB of free chunks below it. In the lab box RSS stayed at 195 MB until that last block was freed too, then fell to 2 MB at once. C has no garbage collector.

sections.h: malloc buys memory from the kernel in bulk and hands it out in pieces
sections.body:
Asking the kernel for memory costs about 6 to 11 µs a time in the lab box: `bulk.c` times 100,000 rounds of `mmap` for one page, one write and `munmap`. A `malloc`, a write and a `free` of 64 bytes takes about 20 ns. That's a factor of several hundred, and a JVM, a database driver or a C library makes millions of small allocations. So `malloc` is not a system call. It's library code inside your process (glibc's, in the lab box) that gets memory from the kernel in big pieces and hands it out in small ones.

Start with the simplest allocator that works: a bump pointer. The library takes a big region, keeps a pointer to the first unused byte, and on each `malloc(n)` returns the pointer and moves it forward by n bytes. When the region runs out, it asks the kernel for more. On Linux the classic way to ask is `brk`, a system call that moves the end of the heap region, called the **program break**. Bump allocation is as fast as allocation gets, but it has no `free`. A service that allocates and frees a 1 KB buffer per request would grow by 1 KB per request, forever.

So the allocator has to remember what was freed. glibc stores an 8-byte size field right before each block; block and header together are a **chunk**. `free(p)` reads the size and puts the chunk on a free list. `malloc(n)` looks for a free chunk that fits and splits off what it doesn't need. Two free chunks that sit side by side merge into one, so three neighbouring 1,000-byte holes can serve a 3,000-byte request. The free space after the last chunk, up to the break, is the **top chunk**. When nothing on the free lists fits, `malloc` carves from the top chunk, and when that runs out it calls `brk` again and takes 128 KB extra, so the next hundred small requests need no system call.

Big requests take another road. A chunk of 128 KB or more that doesn't fit gets its own `mmap`, and `free` hands it straight back with `munmap`. That's the only memory that leaves the process the moment you free it. glibc then raises the threshold to the size of the block it just freed (up to 32 MB), betting that the program will ask for that size again.

The trace of `sizes.c` shows all of it. The first `malloc(1000)` moves the break up by 135,168 bytes: the chunk plus 128 KB, rounded up to pages. Another 1,000 bytes and a 100 KB block come from the top chunk with no system call. 200 KB and 1 MB get their own `mmap`. Freeing the 1 MB block unmaps it, and the next 1 MB request, now under the raised threshold, grows the heap with `brk` instead.

Real glibc doesn't scan one long list. It sorts free chunks into bins by size, and since glibc 2.26 every thread also has a small cache (tcache) of up to 7 freed chunks per size, for sizes up to 1,032 bytes, which it reuses without taking a lock.

try.title: Price a system call per allocation, then watch malloc's calls
steps: `os/c/l08/bulk.c` times one-page `mmap` + write + `munmap` against `malloc` + write + `free`. `os/c/l08/sizes.c` asks for 1,000 bytes twice, 100 KB, 200 KB and 1 MB, frees the 1 MB block and asks for 1 MB again, printing a marker line before each step.
Predict which steps of `sizes.c` make a system call, and which call. Then run both in the lab box. The `sed` drops the program's start-up and keeps the lines from the first marker on.

The first `brk` moves the break by `0x21000`, 135,168 bytes: 1,008 for the chunk plus 128 KB of top pad, rounded up to pages. The second 1,000 bytes and the 100 KB come from that top chunk. 200 KB doesn't fit what's left and is over the 128 KB threshold, so it gets its own mapping of 51 pages. After `munmap` of the 1 MB block the threshold is 1,052,672 bytes, so the second 1 MB request is under it and the break moves up by `0x119000` instead.

sections.h: Freeing memory gives it back to malloc, not to the kernel
sections.body:
`frag.c` allocates 200,000 blocks of 1,000 bytes, about 192 MB of heap, and its RSS (resident set size: its pages in RAM, lesson 6) reaches 195 MB. Then it frees 97% of the blocks, keeping one in every 32. RSS stays at 195 MB.

Nothing leaked. `free` gave every chunk back to `malloc`, which merged the neighbours into free chunks of about 31 KB and keeps them for the next `malloc`. What `free` doesn't do is give pages back to the kernel, and two things stand in the way. The stepper shows both on a small heap.

The first is the shape of the heap. `brk` only moves the end of one contiguous region, so the heap can shrink only from the top. glibc does shrink it: when the top chunk grows past 128 KB (`M_TRIM_THRESHOLD`), `free` moves the break down and keeps 128 KB spare. But one live block near the end pins everything below it. Run `frag.c` keeping only the very last block, and RSS still stays at 195 MB, with 192 MB of free chunks under that one block. Free the last block too, and RSS drops to 2 MB at once.

The second is that the pages of a free chunk are still mapped and still hold data. To return a page from the middle of the heap, the allocator has to tell the kernel it no longer needs the contents, with `madvise(MADV_DONTNEED)`. The address stays valid, the frame goes back to the kernel, and the next touch gets a zeroed page (lesson 6's first-touch fault). glibc does this only when you call `malloc_trim(0)`. It walks every free chunk and releases each whole page inside it, keeping the chunk's first 48 bytes, where the free-list pointers live. In `frag.c` each free run of about 31 KB holds 6 or 7 whole pages, so RSS falls from 195 MB to 33 MB, while the heap still spans 192 MB of addresses.

This is **fragmentation**: free memory broken into pieces. `malloc` can reuse a piece for a block that fits, but the kernel can't take back a page that shares its 4 KB with a live block. A long-running service that builds a big structure and then keeps a few survivors looks exactly like `frag.c`: RSS climbs to the peak and stays near it, even though the program has freed most of what it allocated.

sections.h: One heap per thread: arenas trade memory for less waiting
sections.body:
`arenas.c` starts 16 threads. One at a time, each allocates 16 MB in 4,000-byte blocks and frees all but its last block. With glibc's defaults, the process ends with RSS 253 MB. With `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=1` it ends with 17 MB.

The reason is a lock. A heap with free lists is shared state, so `malloc` and `free` must hold a lock while they change it. With a single heap, threads that allocate at the same moment queue for that lock. In one run of the same program, 16 threads doing 200,000 `malloc`/`free` pairs each took 1.4 s with one heap and 0.18 s with glibc's defaults.

glibc's answer is more heaps. An **arena** is a complete heap with its own lock, its own free lists and its own top chunk. The main thread uses the main arena, the `brk` heap. Any other thread gets an arena at its first `malloc`: a new one while there are fewer than the limit, after that a share of an existing one. The limit is 8 per CPU on 64-bit Linux, so 96 on the lab box's 12 CPUs. A thread keeps the arena it got. Extra arenas live in their own `mmap`ed regions, and each reserves 64 MB of addresses: VSZ (all reserved address space, lesson 6) was 1,155 MB with 17 arenas and 146 MB with one.

The price is that free memory belongs to an arena. When thread 1 frees its 16 MB, the chunks go back on its arena's free lists, and thread 2, allocating from a different arena, can't reuse them. Each arena keeps its own peak. Sixteen threads that each needed 16 MB at a different moment end up holding 16 × 16 MB. With one arena, each thread reuses the chunks the previous one freed, and the process holds one peak.

`MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` sets the limit through the environment, and it must be set before the process starts. For a JVM with hundreds of threads that each touch native memory now and then, a small value such as 2 or 4 is worth trying. It costs more waiting on arena locks, which matters only if native allocation is hot: here 2 arenas gave 33 MB and 0.21 s. Another way out is a different allocator: jemalloc and tcmalloc can be loaded with `LD_PRELOAD`, and they make their own choices about when to hand memory back to the kernel.

sections.h: A JVM's RSS is its heap plus native memory, and NMT sees only part of it
sections.body:
`NativeChurn` starts a JVM with a 64 MB heap, touched up front (`-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch`, lesson 6), and lets 16 threads take turns creating 64 `java.util.zip.Deflater` objects each and ending all but one. The JVM's own accounting says it has 145 MB committed. The kernel says the process has 309 MB of anonymous memory in RAM.

A JVM gets all its memory from `mmap` and `malloc`, like any other process. The Java heap is one big `mmap`, reserved at `-Xmx` (lesson 6). Around it sit the other parts: class metadata (metaspace), the code cache that holds JIT-compiled code, a stack for every thread (lesson 3), the garbage collector's bookkeeping, symbol tables and many smaller `malloc`s. When RSS is bigger than the heap, the question is which of these it is.

**Native Memory Tracking** (NMT) answers that for the JVM's own parts. Start the JVM with `-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary` (Oracle's documentation puts the cost at 5 to 10% performance), and `jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary` prints one line per category, each with `reserved` (address space, like VSZ) and `committed` (memory the JVM has made usable). Committed is an upper bound on what's in RAM: a committed heap page that was never touched isn't in RSS, which is why this demo pre-touches its heap.

NMT counts what HotSpot itself allocates, and nothing else. Its documentation says so: it doesn't track third-party native code or the JDK's class libraries. Each `Deflater` holds zlib's compression state, about 260 KB that zlib gets from `malloc` in the calling thread. So 1,024 of them went through 16 arenas, and NMT saw none of it. Ending them freed the chunks into their arenas, which kept them, as in section 3. The same goes for Netty's native transport, JNI drivers, RocksDB and anything else that calls `malloc` from C.

So read a JVM's memory in three layers. RSS, split into `RssAnon` and `RssFile`, is what the kernel and the container's limit count. NMT's committed total is what HotSpot accounts for. The difference is native code outside HotSpot plus memory the allocator kept after `free`: about 160 MB here. Setting `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2` cut RSS from 320 MB to 145 MB, and NMT's numbers didn't change at all.

```text
RssFile:	   18948 kB
```

NMT's numbers are the same in both runs, to the MB: its `malloc` line counts only HotSpot's own 24 MB of `malloc` calls. `RssAnon` fell by about 175 MB, all of it zlib memory that 16 arenas had kept after `end()`. `RSS at start` is already 110 MB because the 64 MB heap is pre-touched.

analogy: `malloc` is a restaurant kitchen that buys from a wholesaler (the kernel) by the crate and portions it out to the cooks. Leftovers go back in the kitchen's own fridge, not back to the wholesaler, so the kitchen's stock (RSS) stays at the size of the busiest night. Arenas are separate fridges, one per cook, so nobody queues at a single door, but every fridge fills up with its own cook's leftovers, and one cook can't use another's. `malloc_trim` is clearing out every shelf that holds nothing at all. The analogy breaks on what can be given back. A kitchen can return any amount of anything; the kernel takes memory back only in whole 4 KB pages, and a single live block on a page keeps the whole page.
in_your_world: A Kafka consumer service that decompresses zstd or snappy batches goes through JNI libraries (zstd-jni, snappy-java) that allocate with `malloc` in whichever consumer or worker thread runs them. A settlement job that gzips files uses `GZIPOutputStream`, which is `Deflater`, which is zlib's `malloc`. In a pod with 200 threads, that native memory spreads over dozens of arenas, and RSS climbs for hours after a deploy while the heap graphs stay flat and NMT shows nothing growing. It looks like a leak, and the container's limit (lesson 7) treats it as one. Check the arenas before you hunt: `pmap -x` shows them as anonymous regions at 64 MB-aligned addresses, and running with `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2` set in the Deployment's environment often brings RSS down to what the service really needs.
mistake: Calling flat-topped RSS a leak, or the reverse, reading the heap size as the JVM's memory. RSS that rises to the peak of a busy period and then stays there is what malloc does by design: freed chunks go back to its free lists and arenas, and only memory at the top of a heap or in its own `mmap` returns to the kernel. Raising `-Xmx` doesn't help, because the growth isn't in the Java heap. Measure instead. Take an NMT baseline (`jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline`) and compare later with `summary.diff`: a category that keeps growing under steady load is a leak inside the JVM. If NMT is flat and RSS isn't, the memory is native code or allocator overhead: count the arenas with `pmap -x`, and try `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX`. Only RSS that keeps growing under steady load, with no plateau, is a real leak.

compare.title: pmap -x of the same JVM: glibc's default arenas against MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2
compare.note: Both lists show the 62 MB Java heap at `0xfc000000`. On the left, sixteen arenas sit at addresses that end in `000000`, 64 MB apart, each holding 13 MB of zlib memory that was freed but kept. On the right there are two: the `brk` heap (the `0xaaaa...` address, next to the program) and one extra arena, each holding about one thread's peak. VSZ falls from 4.5 GB to 1.8 GB and RSS from 327 MB to 148 MB. Nothing in the Java code changed.

worked.title: Account for a JVM's RSS, layer by layer

steps.say: Start with the kernel's totals and their split. Anonymous memory is heap, stacks and malloc; file pages are mostly the JVM's own libraries and the CDS archive.
steps.code:
grep -E '^(VmRSS|RssAnon|RssFile)' /proc/$pid/status
# VmRSS:	  327696 kB
# RssAnon:	  308780 kB
# RssFile:	   18916 kB

steps.say: Ask the JVM what it allocated, by category. This needs `-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary` at start-up. The heap is pre-touched here, so its 64 MB committed is all in RAM.
steps.code:
jcmd $pid VM.native_memory summary scale=MB | grep -E '^Total|^-'
# Total: reserved=1523MB, committed=145MB
# -                 Java Heap (reserved=64MB, committed=64MB)
# -                     Class (reserved=1024MB, committed=0MB)
# -                    Thread (reserved=54MB, committed=1MB)
# -                      Code (reserved=244MB, committed=8MB)
# -                        GC (reserved=54MB, committed=54MB)
# -        Shared class space (reserved=16MB, committed=14MB, readonly=0MB)
# -                 Metaspace (reserved=64MB, committed=1MB)
# (smaller categories trimmed)

steps.say: Subtract. About 309 MB of anonymous RAM against 145 MB that HotSpot accounts for: roughly 160 MB belongs to native code outside HotSpot or to memory malloc kept after `free`. NMT can't say which, so look at the mappings: arenas show up as anonymous regions on 64 MB boundaries, about 13 MB resident each here.

Change the allocator's policy, not the Java code, and measure again. In a container image or a Kubernetes Deployment it's one environment variable. Here RSS went from 320 MB to 145 MB with NMT unchanged.

ENV MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2
# or in the Deployment: env: [{ name: MALLOC_ARENA_MAX, value: "2" }]

lab.title: Build glibc-style malloc and free, then arenas
steps: Open the three captured files: the `sizes.c` trace and the `frag.c` and `arenas.c` runs from this lesson. The tests replay each one on your model: the same system calls in the same order, RSS within a megabyte or two, the same number of arenas.

Read `Malloc.kt`. `Sizes` has glibc's sizes. In `Heap`, the free chunks live in `freeChunks` (address to size, in address order) and chunks in use in `used`; `trim`, `shrink`, `grow`, `mmapChunk`, `unmap` and `touch` are written for you.
Run the tests from the `labs` folder. All seven fail.
Write `Heap.malloc` in the four steps its KDoc lists: first fit with a split, the top chunk, `mmapChunk`, `grow`.
Write `Heap.free`: unmap, or merge with the free neighbours on both sides and either join the top chunk (and maybe `shrink(topPad)`) or go back in `freeChunks`.
Write `Arenas.arenaFor`. Then look at the arena test's three runs side by side: the same frees, three very different RSS figures.
hints: `freeChunks.entries.firstOrNull { it.value >= size }` is first fit, because a `TreeMap` iterates in address order.
The top chunk is too small when `brk - top < size + Sizes.MIN_CHUNK`. Only then do you choose between `mmapChunk` (size at or over `mmapThreshold`) and `grow`.

In `free`, the chunk after yours starts at `start + size`, so `freeChunks.remove(start + size)` merges it in one call. The chunk before is `freeChunks.lowerEntry(start)`, but only if it ends exactly at `start`.
If the merged chunk ends at `top`, move `top` down to its start and don't add it to `freeChunks`. Call `shrink(topPad)` when `brk - top >= trimThreshold`.

drill.title: Predict malloc's system calls
drill.prompt: A fresh process on glibc runs the five lines below. For each line, write the system call it makes, if any, as a comment. Assume the default thresholds and that each block's pointer is kept.

answer.src:
char *a = malloc(64);           // brk +132 KB: the first chunk plus 128 KB of top pad
char *b = malloc(64 * 1024);    // none: 64 KB fits in the top chunk
char *c = malloc(512 * 1024);   // mmap of 516 KB: over the 128 KB threshold, too big for the top
free(c);                        // munmap; the threshold rises to 516 KB
char *d = malloc(512 * 1024);   // brk: now under the threshold, and the top chunk is too small

recap: `malloc` is library code, not a system call: it gets memory from the kernel with `brk` (moving the program break) or `mmap`, and hands it out in chunks, each with a size header.
Freed chunks go on malloc's free lists and merge with free neighbours. Requests of 128 KB or more that don't fit get their own `mmap` and are unmapped on `free`; glibc then raises that threshold.
The `brk` heap shrinks only from the top, so one live block can pin megabytes of free chunks in RSS. `malloc_trim(0)` returns whole free pages from the middle with `madvise`.
glibc gives threads separate arenas (up to 8 per CPU) to avoid lock waits. Each arena keeps its own freed memory, so RSS can hold one peak per arena. `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` caps them.
A JVM's RSS is the heap plus metaspace, code cache, stacks, GC data and native allocations. NMT shows HotSpot's part; the rest is native libraries and allocator overhead.

quiz.q: From lesson 6: right after `/tmp/frag 32` calls `malloc_trim(0)`, its heap still spans 192 MB of addresses but RSS is 33 MB. What happened to the other pages?
options: They were written to swap
The kernel took back their frames; the addresses are still mapped, and touching one again takes a minor fault and gets a zeroed page
They were compacted: malloc moved the live blocks together
They still hold their data, but `ps` stops counting pages that are free in malloc
quiz.why: `madvise(MADV_DONTNEED)` drops the page-table entries and frees the frames, but leaves the region in place. The next access is a first touch again: a minor fault that maps a zeroed frame. Nothing went to disk, and C's malloc can't move live blocks, because the program holds raw pointers to them.

quiz.q: A service mallocs a 64 KB buffer for each request and frees it when the request ends. After a busy hour its RSS stays 300 MB higher than at start-up, then stays flat for days under steady load. Most likely?
options: A memory leak in the request path
The kernel forgot to reclaim the pages
Freed chunks sitting in malloc's free lists and arenas at the busy hour's peak, reused by later requests
The 64 KB buffers are mmapped and never unmapped
quiz.why: 64 KB is under the 128 KB mmap threshold, so the buffers come from heaps that keep their freed chunks. RSS rises to the peak and stays there, and later requests reuse the chunks, so it doesn't grow further. A leak would keep growing under steady load. An mmapped block would go back to the kernel on `free`.

quiz.q: A JVM with 300 platform threads runs on a 4-CPU VM. Its threads use a JNI compression library now and then. How many glibc arenas can that library's `malloc` calls end up spread over, with default settings?
options: 1: the JVM has a single native heap
4: one per CPU
300: one per thread
Up to 32: 8 per CPU on 64-bit, after which threads share
quiz.why: glibc creates a new arena for a thread's first `malloc` until it reaches 8 × CPUs on 64-bit Linux, then assigns existing ones. In a container with only a CPU quota, glibc still counts the host's CPUs, so the limit can be much higher. `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` sets it explicitly.

quiz.q: NMT's committed total for a JVM stays at 600 MB for a day, while RSS climbs from 700 MB to 1.4 GB. Where should you look first?
options: At memory outside HotSpot: native libraries' `malloc` and what the allocator keeps after `free`, for example with `pmap -x` and `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX`
At the Java heap: take a heap dump
At metaspace: classes are leaking
Nowhere: NMT is the true number and RSS is overcounting
quiz.why: NMT tracks only HotSpot's own allocations, heap and metaspace included, and those are flat. The growth is in memory NMT can't see: JNI and JDK native libraries such as zlib, and freed chunks held by glibc. RSS is what the kernel and the container limit count, so it's the number that gets the pod killed.

quiz.q: A C service allocates a 2 MB buffer per batch and frees it after. Strace shows `mmap` and `munmap` on the first batch, but from the second batch on, no system calls at all. Why?
options: The kernel caches the last unmapped region
Freeing the 2 MB mmapped block raised glibc's mmap threshold above 2 MB, so later buffers come from the heap and are reused there
strace stops tracing after the first call of each type
glibc maps 2 MB with huge pages, which strace can't see
quiz.why: glibc's dynamic threshold: freeing an mmapped block bigger than the threshold (and at most 32 MB) raises the threshold to that block's size. The next 2 MB request is under it, grows the heap once with `brk`, and after that each free and malloc reuses the same chunk without calling the kernel.

flashcards.back: Moves the program break, the end of the process's heap region. glibc's main arena grows and shrinks the heap with it.

flashcards.front: When does glibc use `mmap` for a single `malloc`?
flashcards.back: When the chunk is at least the mmap threshold (128 KB at start, raised dynamically up to 32 MB) and doesn't fit in the free lists or the top chunk.

flashcards.front: Why can RSS stay high after `free`?
flashcards.back: Freed chunks stay on malloc's free lists, and the brk heap shrinks only from the top. Only whole free pages at the top, or with `malloc_trim`, go back to the kernel.
Gives back every whole page inside free chunks (with `madvise`) and trims the top of the heap. Addresses stay; RAM goes.

flashcards.front: What is a glibc arena, and the default limit?
flashcards.back: A separate heap with its own lock and free lists, given to threads to cut contention. Default limit: 8 × CPUs on 64-bit; set with `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX`.
Memory allocated by native code outside HotSpot (JDK libraries like zlib, JNI libraries) and memory glibc keeps after `free`.

terms.plain: The end of a process's heap region; the `brk` system call moves it up or down.
A block handed out by malloc plus its hidden size header; the unit malloc splits, frees and merges.
The free space at the end of a heap, up to the break, that malloc carves from when its free lists have nothing that fits.
Free memory split into pieces: too small for a request, or sharing pages with live blocks so the kernel can't take them back.
One of glibc's separate heaps, each with its own lock, so threads don't all wait on one.
The size from which glibc gives a request its own mapping instead of carving it from a heap.
Native Memory Tracking: HotSpot's accounting of its own native memory, by category, read with jcmd.

explain_back.prompt: Your Quarkus service's pod shows RSS of 1.4 GB with `-Xmx512m`, NMT says about 700 MB committed, and RSS never comes down after the morning peak. A teammate wants to raise the memory limit and call it a leak. Explain what's going on and what you'd try first.
explain_back.answer: The heap is only one part of what the kernel counts. NMT's 700 MB covers HotSpot's own memory: the 512 MB heap plus metaspace, code cache, thread stacks and GC structures. The other 700 MB is memory HotSpot didn't allocate itself, so NMT can't see it. That's native libraries calling `malloc` (compression, JNI drivers, Netty's native parts) and, very often, glibc keeping memory after `free`. glibc gives each thread an arena, up to 8 per CPU, and freed chunks go back to their arena's free lists, not to the kernel. A heap can only shrink from the top, so each arena holds on to its own peak. That's why RSS rises to the morning peak and then stays flat: it's reused, not leaked. A leak would keep climbing under steady load. I'd check with `pmap -x` for many anonymous regions on 64 MB boundaries, take an NMT baseline and a `summary.diff` later to prove the JVM's own categories are flat, and then set `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2` in the Deployment's environment and compare RSS under the same load. Raising the limit only hides it until the next peak.

deeper.body:
The tcache that glibc added in 2.26 is a per-thread array of 64 lists, one per 16-byte size class up to 1,032 bytes, each holding up to 7 freed chunks. A `free` of a small block puts it on its thread's list with no lock, and the next `malloc` of the same size takes it right back. That's why `bulk.c`'s 64-byte `malloc` and `free` cost about 20 ns, and why `arenas.c` uses 4,000-byte blocks: smaller ones would never reach the arena's lock.

The arena heaps are visible in `/proc/<pid>/maps`. glibc reserves each one as a 64 MB region aligned to 64 MB, made inaccessible (`---p`) except for the part in use, which it opens up with `mprotect` as the arena grows. That's the `16776` KB `rw---` region at each 64 MB boundary in the `pmap` output above; the rest of the 64 MB is the reserved part. Alignment lets `free` find a chunk's arena from its address alone, by rounding down to 64 MB.

glibc's limits can be changed without recompiling. `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX`, `MALLOC_TRIM_THRESHOLD_`, `MALLOC_TOP_PAD_` and `MALLOC_MMAP_THRESHOLD_` (note the trailing underscores on the last three) map to the `mallopt` parameters, and newer glibc versions read the same settings as tunables through `GLIBC_TUNABLES`. Setting any of the last three switches the dynamic mmap threshold off.

The JVM can show you the allocator's side too. `jcmd <pid> System.native_heap_info` prints glibc's `malloc_info` XML, with one `<heap nr=...>` element per arena, the same report `arenas.c` counts. `jcmd <pid> System.trim_native_heap` makes glibc run `malloc_trim` inside a live JVM, which is a quick test of how much of RSS is free chunks. On a `NativeChurn` JVM started without NMT it printed `Trim native heap: RSS+Swap: 262M->61652K (-202M)`: 200 MB that only looked like a leak.
